title: Water
objective: After this level you can explain what makes the water molecule so special.
summary: Water is polar: oxygen pulls shared electrons harder. Hydrogen bonds between molecules make water boil at 100 °C, not about −80 °C, give it surface tension and hold ice's open lattice.

cards.headline: By the pattern of similar compounds, water should boil at about −80 °C.
cards.body: It boils at 100 °C instead. If water followed the pattern, the drink in your glass would be a gas at room temperature. The explanation is one lopsided little molecule.

cards.headline: A lopsided molecule
cards.body: Inside a water molecule, the atoms share electrons, but not fairly. Oxygen pulls harder, so its end of the molecule carries a slight negative charge, and the two hydrogen ends carry slight positive charges. The hydrogens sit at an angle of about 104.5°, not in a straight line, so the molecule has a negative side and a positive side. Chemists call that polar.
cards.callout: Polar: slightly negative at one end, slightly positive at the other

cards.headline: Molecules that cling
cards.body: The positive hydrogen end of one water molecule is drawn to the negative oxygen end of its neighbor. That pull between molecules is a hydrogen bond. Each one is much weaker than the bonds inside a molecule, but a glass of water is full of them. Remember Level 4? To boil, particles must break away from their neighbors. For water, that means breaking hydrogen bonds, which is why it boils at 100 °C, not −80 °C.

mascot.line: Keep this: one lopsided molecule explains the high boiling point, the pond's skin and floating ice.

cards.headline: A skin on the pond
cards.body: All that clinging gives water's surface a kind of skin, called surface tension. It's strong enough for water striders to walk across a pond, and it can even float a steel paper clip.

cards.headline: Level 8's ice, explained
cards.body: Remember Level 8's floating ice? When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open lattice that holds them farther apart than in the liquid. Same mass, more space: ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats. Icebergs bob on the sea because of a lopsided molecule.

cards.headline: Water: decoded
learned: Water is polar: negative oxygen end, positive hydrogen ends
Hydrogen bonds pull neighboring molecules together
They make water boil at 100 °C, not about −80 °C
They give water surface tension and hold ice's open lattice

questions.prompt: In a water molecule, which part carries a slight negative charge?

options.label: The two hydrogen ends
options.rationale: The hydrogen ends are slightly positive.

options.label: No part, because its charge is spread evenly
options.rationale: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder, so the charge is uneven.

options.label: Only the gap between the two hydrogens
options.rationale: The negative charge sits at the oxygen end.

questions.explanation: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive.

questions.prompt: Why does water boil at 100 °C when similar compounds suggest about −80 °C?

options.label: Its molecules are much heavier than similar ones
options.rationale: Weight isn't the reason; the pull between molecules is.

options.label: Its covalent bonds must break before it can boil
options.rationale: Boiling separates whole molecules; the bonds inside stay.

options.label: The air always presses harder on water
options.rationale: Air pressure is the same for water and its cousins.

options.label: Hydrogen bonds between molecules must be broken

questions.explanation: To boil, water molecules must break free of the hydrogen bonds that hold them to their neighbors, which takes much more heat.

questions.prompt: Level 8 said ice floats because frozen water forms an open lattice. What holds that lattice open?

options.label: Air bubbles trapped inside the ice
options.rationale: Solid ice floats without any trapped air.

options.label: Salt that was dissolved in the water
options.rationale: Pure ice floats too; salt isn't the reason.

options.label: Ice molecules being bigger than water ones
options.rationale: Ice and liquid water are the same molecules.

questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds lock frozen water molecules into an open lattice, spreading them out so ice is less dense than liquid water.
